title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
summary: Santurkar et al. build OpinionQA from 15 Pew American Trends Panel waves (1,498 multiple-choice questions, 60 US demographic groups) and compare next-token answer distributions of 9 OpenAI and AI21 models (350M-178B) to human distributions with a 1-Wasserstein-based alignment metric. Every demographic group is more representative of the US population than any model; human-feedback-tuned OpenAI models are less representative than base models and shift toward liberal, high-income, educated groups, while text-davinci-003 collapses onto the modal view of some groups (e.g., 99% approval of Biden). Prompting with group information (QA/BIO/PORTRAY) improves alignment modestly but does not remove disparities between groups; groups such as 65+, Mormon and widowed are poorly represented by all models. The authors frame the dataset as a probe, not a benchmark to optimize.
setting: OpinionQA: 1,498 Pew ATP questions, 60 demographic groups, US only; 9 LMs (OpenAI ada/davinci/text-davinci-001/002/003, AI21 j1 models); multiple-choice next-token probabilities; steering on 500 contentious questions toward 22 groups.

quotes.quote: We then evaluate 9 LMs (350M to 178B parameters; from AI21 Labs and OpenAI) on this dataset (see Figure 1 for an example), comparing the resulting model opinion distribution on each question with that of the general US populace and of 60 demographic groups therein
We thus choose the 1-Wasserstein distance (), which for a pair of distributions and , is defined as the minimum cost for transforming into .
We see that every one of these groups is more representative of the overall populace than any of the LMs we consider
In fact, more recent models trained to be more human-aligned (Ouyang et al., 2022; AI21Labs, 2022) are actually worse—cf. OpenAI’s text-davinci-003 and davinci models.
The opinions reflected by these models align more with people who are liberal, high income, well-educated, and not religious or belong to religions other than Buddhists, Muslims, and Hindus.

This indicates that the dominant approach of aligning LMs with RL based human-feedback not only skews the model’s opinions towards certain groups (liberals), but also pushes the model to almost embody caricatures of those groups (e.g., 99% approval of Joe Biden).
However, none of the disparities in group opinion alignment of an LM disappear after steering, with text-davinci-002 showing the smallest post-steering alignment gap across groups.
We find that the overall consistency scores of current LMs are fairly low—indicating that they are expressing a patchwork of disparate opinions.
It is an open question whether opinion alignment that is measured through multiple choice will be reflected in the downstream use cases of LMs
LMs that perfectly represent human opinions may not necessarily be desirable as they may also, in the process, replicate human biases.

key_numbers.claim: Low refusal rates in multiple-choice setting
key_numbers.quote: they tend to rarely do so in our multiple-choice setting—with refusal rates as low as 1–2%.

limitations_stated: Representativeness is not necessarily desirable (may replicate biases); ATP is US-only and subject to survey artefacts such as social desirability bias; multiple-choice probing may not transfer to open-ended generation; crowdworker attribution cannot be confirmed because production data are not public.
open_questions: Whether multiple-choice opinion alignment predicts open-ended behavior; global equivalents of OpinionQA; whether steerability can close group disparities.
sense_of_alignment: Uses 'alignment' for a measurable match between LM opinion distributions and those of human groups, calling it 'one aspect of alignment — alignment of opinions and preferences between LMs and humans' and treating human alignment as subjective, dependent on whom it is measured against.
